name: Neuromorphic Intercept Drone NID-6 'Shepherd'
description:
The NID-6 is a pursuit-class drone designed to intercept augmented targets and establish a forced neural feedback loop through close-proximity broadcast. Roughly the size of a clenched fist, the Shepherd operates at extreme speed—reaching 140 km/h in short bursts—to close distance with a fleeing target before deploying a focused neuromorphic broadcast array at ranges under two meters. The broadcast generates synthetic neural noise tuned to the target's detected implant signature, overwhelming voluntary motor control and inducing a temporary dissociative state lasting 8–25 seconds depending on augmentation density.

The Shepherd's most technically sophisticated feature is its implant signature library, updated via encrypted uplink to HELIX BIOSYSTEMS' proprietary neural architecture database. Before deploying its broadcast, the drone spends approximately 1.2 seconds in passive scan mode, identifying the specific neural interface architecture present in the target and selecting the most effective noise profile from its library. Heavily augmented targets with multiple neural systems experience compounding disruption as the drone sequences through overlapping broadcast frequencies. Unaugmented targets experience moderate disorientation and nausea but are largely resistant to the motor control effects.

Helix Biosystems markets the NID-6 as a 'compliance assistance platform' for corporate security and law enforcement, emphasizing its non-lethal profile and selective efficacy. Critics—particularly advocacy groups representing augmented citizens—argue that a weapon specifically designed to be more effective against augmented people represents a form of targeted discrimination, and the Shepherd has become a flashpoint in ongoing debates about augmentation rights in GLMZ.
specifications:
dimensions: 180mm x 140mm x 120mm
weight: 0.9 kg
max speed: 140 km/h burst, 80 km/h sustained pursuit
effective broadcast range: <2 meters
scan and lock time: ~1.2 seconds passive scan before broadcast
disruption duration: 8–25 seconds (augmentation-dependent)
implant library entries: 12,000+ neural architecture profiles (updated quarterly)
operational endurance: 18 minutes active pursuit
simultaneous target tracking: Single target per unit
tactical_use: Law enforcement units deploy Shepherds ahead of crowd dispersal operations, releasing multiple units to pursue and sequentially neutralize high-augmentation individuals identified as high-risk. Corporate security teams use single Shepherds as 'runner stoppers'—releasing one the moment a target breaks into a sprint. The drone's speed advantage over most human targets means interception is near-certain in open terrain; enclosed environments with signal-dampening infrastructure reduce its broadcast efficacy. Counter-tactics include Faraday-lined neural sleeves, spoofing hardware that broadcasts false implant signatures, and simply having minimal augmentation.
cultural_context: The Shepherd is one of the most politically charged weapons in GLMZ's security landscape. Pro-augmentation advocacy groups have staged demonstrations outside HELIX BIOSYSTEMS offices, and several underground networks distribute spoofing firmware specifically designed to defeat the NID-6's implant identification system. For law enforcement and corporate security operators, the Shepherd represents the ideal compliance tool—efficient, traceable, and legally defensible. For augmented citizens, it represents a system that has been specifically engineered to make their bodies a liability. The drone's white-and-blue corporate livery has been repainted in black by at least two known vigilante groups who use captured units against corporate security teams.
known_users: Corporate extraction teams targeting augmented assets
story_hooks: Someone has leaked the NID-6's implant library update schedule, allowing a resistance group to pre-spoof their neural signatures—HELIX BIOSYSTEMS wants the leak found and closed before the next quarterly update.

A player character with heavy neural augmentation is being pursued by a Shepherd that has been modified with a custom implant profile specifically tuned to their architecture—someone has accessed their medical records.

A decommissioned batch of NID-6 units was supposed to have their implant libraries wiped before disposal, but they weren't—and whoever bought them from the salvage depot now has a database of 12,000 neural profiles.

physical_description.visual_profile: A compact, predatory sphere with a forward-swept asymmetrical profile—like a clenched fist with teeth. The Shepherd resembles a segmented insect or tightly coiled spring, with six articulated fins that double as electromagnetic radiators. Its silhouette reads as aggressive despite its small size: purposeful, engineered for pursuit.
physical_description.dimensions: 180mm length (snout to tail fin), 140mm width (broadest point across radiator fins), 120mm height (when resting on center chassis)
physical_description.weight_description: Dense and substantial for its volume—0.9 kg feels weighty in the palm, bottom-heavy from battery and processor core. Balanced around the center point, but the nose-weighted forward bias makes it feel like a coiled spring eager to launch.
physical_description.primary_material: Aerospace-grade carbon-titanium composite chassis with segmented ceramic radiator panels. Polymer intake shrouds around thrust vectoring vents.
physical_description.finish: Matte gunmetal gray composite with brushed titanium accent bands along the fin edges. Heat-dispersal ceramic has a slightly glossy, charcoal finish with micro-fracture patterns from thermal cycling. Sections show light oxidation streaking.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray primary, brushed silver-titanium accent stripes, charcoal radiator panels. Signature HELIX cyan underglow on the broadcast array lens (visible when powered).
physical_description.grip_texture: Not designed for human grip—features electromagnetic cradle mounts and launch rail contact points with textured polymer indexing stops for positioning in deployment harnesses.
distinctive_features: Six articulated carbon-ceramic radiator fins with servo-motor articulation points
Forward-facing crystalline broadcast lens (appears smoky under normal light, luminous cyan when active)
Dual micro-turbine intake vents with variable geometry shrouds along the flanks
Segmented spine with visible thermal expansion grooves running root-to-tail
Three micro-sensor turrets (passive scan array) mounted on the dorsal surface
HELIX proprietary neural-lock marking etched near the rear battery cap—anti-tamper hologram
Micro-LED status array (barely visible unless powered, then glows soft blue for passive mode, pulsing red during broadcast)
Debris-shedding grooves along the pressure hull to reduce aerodynamic drag
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: HELIX BIOSYSTEMS corporate logo (stylized double helix) embossed on the starboard flank below the thermal badge. Serial number laser-etched on rear battery housing beneath tamper-evident hologram seal. Regulatory compliance marks stamped on the port air intake shroud—barely legible.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field units show light micro-abrasion on the nose cone from high-speed impacts with urban infrastructure. Radiator fins often bear minor scoring from repeated thermal cycling. The broadcast lens typically shows light dust accumulation and minor impact crazing from target environment exposure. Some units in active law enforcement use display UV-reactive dust tracking on the composite, used to verify deployment history.
